questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The end of a settler state
questions.learningObjective: Explain why settler states lost political dominance once the majority could vote.
questions.stem: Your architect's brief for a civic centre in Salisbury asks you to explain why a state built by settlers eventually lost the argument over who belonged. Which account is best supported by the record?

options.text: The settler minority could not hold political dominance once the African majority could vote.
The settlers left because international law banned the ownership of land by Europeans.
options.misconception: believes international law barred European landholding

options.text: The settlers left because their government in the capital had already granted them autonomy.
options.misconception: believes the metropolitan government released the settlers first

options.text: The settlers left because the climate made farming unprofitable in the region.
options.misconception: believes climate and farm economics ended the settler state

questions.explanation: Settler states rested on keeping a large population out of the vote, and once exclusion ended the arithmetic worked against them. No law barred landholding, climate did not end it, and the settlers were not released.
questions.hint: Ask what the minority's advantage rested on.

questions.learningObjective: Infer a long metropolitan squeeze from cost and staffing series.
questions.stem: A budget brief in your archive compares the overseas administration costs of the colonial power in 1938, 1955 and 1970: 210 million, 340 million and 95 million units, while the number of overseas administrative posts fell from 41,000 to 44,000 to 9,000. What does this show?

options.text: Administrative costs fell in step with staffing, so spending was never the pressure.
options.misconception: assumes costs and staffing moved together throughout

options.text: Overseas spending rose steadily, so the empire was always affordable to the metropole.
options.misconception: claims overseas spending rose steadily throughout the period

options.text: Costs stayed high for decades while staffing was later cut sharply, exposing a long squeeze.
The empire was inexpensive at the end, so its end was purely a matter of local politics.
options.misconception: assumes cheap administration explains the empire's end

questions.explanation: Costs climbed for two decades then collapsed with the cut in posts, showing a long squeeze on the metropolitan budget before the political decisions. Costs and staffing did not move together.
questions.hint: Compare spending with headcount across the three dates.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why settler and business interests stalled negotiations.
questions.stem: Your design review asks you to explain why negotiations over the future of a settler colony repeatedly stalled in the nineteen-sixties. Which explanation is most persuasive?

options.text: Negotiations stalled because the incoming nationalist leaders had no agreed programme.
options.misconception: blames the deadlock on nationalist leaders lacking a programme

options.text: Settler and business interests blocked any settlement that would alter their property rights.
Negotiations stalled because the metropolitan government refused to supply the mediators.
options.misconception: blames the deadlock on the absence of metropolitan mediators

options.text: Negotiations stalled because the colonial administration had no accurate population records.
options.misconception: blames the deadlock on poor colonial population records

questions.explanation: Groups whose land and business positions were at stake refused terms that would change their status, and no settlement could hold without their consent. Nationalists had programmes, mediators existed, and records were available.
questions.hint: Ask whose interests each proposed term threatened.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why handover terms were settled before independence.
questions.stem: Your building's interpretation suite asks you to explain why the terms of a handover were often negotiated in detail before independence rather than left to the incoming governments.

answer.exemplar: Settling the detail in advance protected both sides from the uncertainties that followed a sudden transfer. The outgoing government could define the assets it handed over, the guarantees it gave and the arrangements for debt, pensions and defence, while the incoming leadership could make its own entry into office unconditional, avoiding the appearance of negotiating away national sovereignty. The handover then became a settled administrative fact rather than an open-ended argument.

questions.explanation: Pre-negotiated terms removed uncertainty for both sides and let the incoming government take office unconditionally, which is why the detail was settled beforehand. Leaving it open risked turning the transfer itself into a permanent dispute.
questions.hint: Focus on certainty for the incoming government.

questions.learningObjective: Characterise a disciplined non-violent campaign from a report.

stimulus.body: The report urges members to refuse the passes that restricted movement, to boycott the stores that sold to the administration, to hold meetings rather than take up arms, and to keep every instruction public so that any leader could be held to it. options.misconception: mischaracterises the campaign as an armed underground struggle

options.text: A boycott and strike movement that avoided all contact with the authorities.
options.misconception: mischaracterises the campaign as avoiding the authorities

options.text: A political campaign that relied on leaders to act on their own judgement.
options.misconception: mischaracterises the campaign as dependent on individual initiative

options.text: Disciplined, public and non-violent organisation rather than armed action.

questions.explanation: Public instructions, refusal of passes, boycotts and a preference for statements over retaliation describe disciplined non-violent organisation that constrained its own leadership. Nothing suggests arms or secrecy.
questions.hint: Notice how the campaign handled arrest and leadership.

options.text: The insurgency was winning, since it had taken most of the country by the end of the year.
options.misconception: reads a shrinking rebel area as a rebel victory

options.text: The government had crushed the insurgency, since the insurgents were confined to a few districts.
options.misconception: claims the insurgency was crushed by government forces

questions.learningObjective: Explain why transition to majority rule was negotiated rather than imposed.
questions.stem: A lecture hall asks you to explain why the transition from settler rule to majority rule in such states was typically negotiated rather than imposed by the departing power. Which reasoning is best?

options.text: The departing power had no choice, because the settlers had already lost the military contest.
options.misconception: claims the settlers had already been militarily defeated

options.text: A negotiated transfer let both sides preserve working institutions and settle their claims.
Negotiated exits were preferred because international courts had ruled against colonial rule.
options.misconception: invents an international court ruling against colonial rule

options.text: The settlers insisted on a negotiated exit because they believed they would win the next election.
options.misconception: claims the settlers expected to win a subsequent election

questions.explanation: A negotiated transfer let the incoming government take power with workable institutions while giving departing settlers guarantees about property, so both sides preferred it. The settlers were not defeated and no court ruled against empire.
questions.hint: Ask what each side gained from a negotiated settlement.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how post-war exhaustion made decolonisation possible and fast.
questions.stem: Your interpretive material asks you to explain why the exhaustion of European powers after the Second World War made decolonisation both possible and fast.

answer.exemplar: The war had left the metropolitan economies indebted, their populations hungry and their governments reluctant to spend on distant garrisons. At the same time the language of self-determination and national liberation had spread far beyond the colonies themselves, so the old claim that colonial rule served a civilising purpose could no longer be made without inviting ridicule. Overwhelmed and embarrassed, the metropolitan states seized on negotiated transfers as the least costly way to end a commitment they could no longer afford.

questions.explanation: Economic exhaustion and a lost ideological argument made withdrawal both feasible and urgent, and negotiated transfers offered the cheapest exit. Decolonisation speed came from metropolitan pressure, not from local weakness alone.
questions.hint: Consider cost and argument together at home.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why elections alone did not produce effective government.
questions.stem: A design review asks you to explain why a new state could hold elections but still fail to govern effectively.

options.text: Because elections choose leaders, while governing needs staff, money and settled rules.
Because the electoral system was borrowed and could not be adapted to local custom.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Negotiating an exit from a guerrilla war
questions.learningObjective: Explain why prisoner and amnesty clauses were central to settlements.
questions.stem: A seminar module asks you to explain why negotiated endings to guerrilla conflicts so often contained a clause on prisoners and amnesty that both sides treated as central.

answer.exemplar: A prisoner and amnesty clause was the one element both a government and an insurgent leadership could defend to their own supporters. For the government it converted an unwinnable war into a lawful transfer of authority, and for the insurgents it converted defeat into a recognised political standing, so that the movement's leaders could claim the campaign had achieved something. Because each side could present the clause as the minimum it had won, the settlement became the part of the agreement that could not be disowned.

questions.explanation: Prisoner and amnesty terms let both sides present the settlement as a gain rather than a defeat, which is why they were rarely the first casualty of negotiation. Military questions proved far harder to settle.
questions.hint: Focus on what each side could claim from the clause.

A conflict between the settlers and the metropolitan government over defence spending.
options.misconception: misreads the exchange as a disagreement over defence budgets

questions.explanation: The first speaker asserts a claim from what was built, the second insists that numbers decide under a parliament, and that collision ended settler predominance. The dispute was not about output, elections or defence spending.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why new states were valuable partners for outside powers.
questions.stem: Your historical interpretation panel asks you to explain why new states in the region became valuable partners for outside powers seeking influence rather than mere trading partners.

answer.exemplar: A newly independent state offered what older colonies did not: a government able to sign treaties, grant port and base facilities and conclude commercial agreements on its own authority, which made it a legal partner rather than an administrative posting. Because such a state could also switch alignment, competing powers competed to court it, and each new agreement carried the risk of pushing the government towards its rivals, which is why influence was won through binding commitments rather than goodwill.

questions.explanation: Sovereignty made new states usable partners for treaties and concessions that older colonies could not offer, and their openness to competing suitors made them worth courting. Influence had to be secured through commitments, not goodwill.
questions.hint: Focus on what sovereignty allowed a new state to do.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why settler organisations were so effective at blocking agreements.
questions.stem: A research seminar weighs two explanations for why settler organisations were so effective at blocking agreements that would have altered their position.

options.text: Because their votes in closely divided parliaments made ministerial support conditional on their consent.
Because settler organisations were funded generously from overseas, which bought their influence.
options.misconception: attributes their leverage to overseas funding

options.text: Because they had better legal representation than any other group in the colony.
options.misconception: credits settler groups with superior legal representation

options.text: Because they controlled the revenue of the districts in which the settlers were concentrated.
options.misconception: claims settler groups controlled district revenue

questions.explanation: Settler organisations were decisive in closely divided metropolitan parliaments, so ministers needed their support and settlers could refuse a settlement altering their position. Funding, legal skill and revenue do not explain it.
questions.hint: Focus on where a minority's leverage is concentrated.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why incoming governments accepted externally drafted clauses.
questions.stem: A reading-room display asks you to explain why new governments in settler colonies so often accepted constitutional clauses written by the departing power's lawyers.

answer.exemplar: The incoming leadership was frequently new to government, working from a short list of advisers with no institutional experience of their own, and the departing power controlled the lawyers, the drafting office and the text that would be presented as the only workable settlement. Accepting that draft spared them the risk of a delay in which the administration ground on without direction, and it allowed them to declare that the constitution had been their own act. Drafting power and political weakness combined to shape the constitution rather than any absence of ideas about how a state should be run.

questions.explanation: New governments with little administrative experience and no drafting resources took the text offered, and the risk of delay without a functioning administration made that tempting. Constitutional design reflected who could draft, not only what was wanted.
questions.hint: Focus on who drafted the text and who was waiting.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Characterise the discipline of a movement from a participant account.

stimulus.body: The account describes months of meetings in which arguments were rehearsed, speakers chosen for their patience rather than their heat, and no decision taken without a written agreement that everyone had approved. It records that the movement refused to nominate leaders for elected office, because it wanted to be judged by what it had done rather than by who spoke for it.

questions.stem: A gallery caption quotes this participant's account. Which aspect of the movement's method does it most clearly illustrate?

options.text: The movement built its case on a single charismatic spokesman with a national following.
options.misconception: contradicts the account's explicit refusal of personal leadership

options.text: The movement depended on spontaneous disorder rather than planned discussion.
options.misconception: contradicts the account's emphasis on planned discussion

options.text: Discipline, deliberative preparation and a refusal of personal leadership.
The movement's aim was to win elected office as the primary route to change.
options.misconception: contradicts the account's rejection of standing for office

questions.explanation: Rehearsed arguments, chosen speakers, written agreements and a refusal to contest elections describe a movement organised around disciplined collective action rather than individuals or office. Nothing suggests charisma or spontaneity.
questions.hint: Notice the account's refusal of official roles.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what made a new state attractive to outside powers.
questions.stem: A research group asks which single feature of a newly independent state made it the most attractive object of outside competition.

options.text: Its sovereignty allowed it to sign binding agreements that older colonies could not.
Its small population made it cheap for an outside power to buy.
options.misconception: reduces the value of a state to the size of its population

options.text: Its lack of infrastructure made it easy for outsiders to build a presence.
options.misconception: treats underdevelopment as the chief attraction

options.text: Its geographical position made it impossible for rivals to divide it.
options.misconception: invents a geography that prevented partition

questions.explanation: Only a government with its own authority could bind itself to treaties, concessions and alignments, which is what made new states attractive. Population size, infrastructure and geography do not explain it.

options.misconception: claims a single universal sequence of settlement steps

questions.learningObjective: Explain why sovereignty and land control could move separately.
questions.stem: A planning seminar asks you to explain why a settler state could lose control of the argument over land while keeping its language, currency and legal system.

options.misconception: explains continuity by the new administration's admiration

options.text: Because recognition of sovereignty and control of land were settled by different instruments.
Because the settlers kept the vote, since they were the largest population in the colony.
options.misconception: claims the settlers held the largest population

options.text: Because the settlers kept their language, since the new government lacked civil servants.
options.misconception: explains continuity by a shortage of trained officials

questions.explanation: Sovereignty was settled by negotiation and recognition while land was settled by law and administration, so a state could gain one and lose the other. Admiration, population size and staffing shortages explain nothing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a changed metropolitan electorate removed the veto on reform.
questions.stem: Your seminar asks you to explain how the loss of a settled imperial majority in the metropolitan electorate removed the veto on reform.

answer.exemplar: A colonial government seeking reform had to carry two audiences: the local population whose demands had to be answered, and a metropolitan electorate that had never accepted the cost of empire. As that electorate changed and the war's memory of scarcity hardened, claims that colonial rule was a duty became claims that it was a luxury, and the parliamentary arithmetic that had sustained overseas budgets began to work against them. What had been an administrative decision for decades therefore became a political impossibility, and reform stopped being a matter of timing.

questions.explanation: A changing metropolitan electorate turned empire from a duty into a cost, removing the political basis for the veto on reform. Administrative convenience alone cannot explain why reform became impossible.
questions.hint: Focus on what the home electorate had stopped accepting.

options.text: Concentrating all decision-making in a single small committee.
options.misconception: contrary to the emphasis on open and collective decisions

options.misconception: contradicts the campaign's openness about its instructions

questions.learningObjective: Interpret rival aid offers as competition for strategic access.

questions.stem: An exhibition panel uses this embassy report. Which reading of the rivalry described is best supported?

options.text: The new state accepted the larger offer because the smaller loan carried fewer conditions.
options.misconception: assumes the state chose the larger offer for fewer conditions

options.text: The two powers had agreed a joint division of the harbour between them.
options.misconception: invents a joint division of the harbour between the two powers

The new state had no interest in either offer and was seeking a third party.
options.misconception: invents a third party that the state was waiting for

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why some inherited institutions outlived others.
questions.stem: A research group asks why some inherited institutions collapsed within months while others survived for decades. Which explanation is most persuasive?

options.text: Because institutions built in the colonial period were always more durable than new ones.
options.misconception: claims colonial-era institutions always outlasted newer ones

options.text: Because the length of colonial rule determined how long institutions survived.
options.misconception: claims length of colonial rule determined institutional survival

options.text: Because institutions with more formal rules were always the most resilient.
options.misconception: claims formality of rules determined institutional resilience

options.text: Because institutions endure only where enough people can make and change them.

questions.explanation: Institutions lasted where people could use, dispute and amend them, because legitimacy and adaptability came from participation rather than age or elaborate rules. Neither colonial origin nor length of rule decided it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Negotiating an exit from a guerrilla war
questions.learningObjective: Explain why armies ended guerrilla wars by negotiation.
questions.stem: Your collection's label text asks you to explain why armies in such conflicts so often ended the war by negotiation rather than by capturing the enemy's capital.

answer.exemplar: Armies fighting dispersed rural forces win battles but rarely win wars, because every operation costs men and money while the enemy can absorb losses and return. Defeat in a decisive battle would not break an organisation whose strength lay in local support and foreign supply, so the rational way to end the war was to buy the other side's agreement through guarantees about prisoners, amnesty and political status. Victory in the field could not produce what a negotiated settlement could.

questions.explanation: Because dispersed opponents could not be decisively beaten and their political support could not be destroyed by a battle, armies bought an end through guarantees rather than military victory. Cost and futility drove that choice.
questions.hint: Focus on why a decisive battle would not end the conflict.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why handover clauses favoured the outgoing administration.
questions.stem: A teaching session asks you to explain why the terms agreed at handover tended to protect the outgoing administration more than the incoming one.

answer.exemplar: The people who drafted the settlement were the officials of the departing administration, and they knew which files mattered and which obligations the new government would find difficult to honour. They wrote clauses on pensions, on liabilities and on the phased handover of assets that made their own position predictable and the incoming ministry's obligations open ended. The incoming leadership accepted these terms in exchange for recognition, speed and an end to the uncertainty in which the administration might otherwise have stalled.

questions.explanation: The departing officials drafted the terms and knew the state's obligations best, so clauses favoured them, and the incoming side paid for speed and recognition. The imbalance came from drafting power.

options.text: The restrictions targeted the campaign's ordinary methods, while leaving a channel for petitioning open.
The proclamation was drafted in response to demands the campaign had already won.
options.misconception: claims the restrictions followed a campaign victory

options.text: The proclamation shows the authorities had decided to abandon the campaign entirely.
options.misconception: reads the restrictions as a decision to give up

questions.explanation: Bans on gatherings and processions hit the campaign's ordinary methods, while the promise of daily petitions kept a lawful route open, which is why the restrictions were temporary and reviewable. No victory or abandonment is evidenced.
questions.hint: Ask what the proclamation restricted and what it left open.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer competing sponsors from diverging assistance figures.
questions.stem: A programme table you are auditing shows foreign military assistance to three new states in 1972 and 1977: the first rose from 40 to 95 units, the second fell from 70 to 25, and the third moved from 30 to 33. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: All three states had changed their alignment away from their original sponsors.
options.misconception: assumes a change in aid levels proves a change of alignment

options.text: The third state's figures show that external aid was growing everywhere in the region.
options.misconception: generalises one state's change to the whole region

options.text: The figures show that military assistance was irrelevant to political alignment.
options.misconception: claims aid levels had no bearing on political alignment

options.text: Assistance moved in different directions, suggesting sponsors competing for influence.

questions.explanation: One state gaining, one losing and one roughly static suggests sponsors competing for position rather than a regional trend in aid. A change in aid levels does not prove a change of alignment.
questions.hint: Compare the three columns before generalising.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why electoral majorities did not deliver administrative control.
questions.stem: While reviewing ministry papers in your archive, you must explain why a government elected by a majority of the population could still be unable to control the territory it governed.

options.text: Because the colonial state deliberately withheld officials from its successor.
options.misconception: invents a deliberate withholding of officials after independence

options.text: Because electoral majorities and effective administrative control were different things.
Because international observers had questioned the validity of the poll.
options.misconception: invents international observers questioning the poll

options.text: Because the new state had chosen a parliamentary system rather than a presidency.
options.misconception: treats the choice of system as the explanation for failure

questions.explanation: Winning votes and governing a territory are different tasks, and where administrative machinery and money had not been built, an elected majority could not command the country. Withholding, observer doubts and system choice explain none.
questions.hint: Ask what an elected majority actually gives a government.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Negotiating an exit from a guerrilla war
questions.learningObjective: Infer how fighting levels and talks length relate in an exit.
questions.stem: A negotiation monitor's report you are reviewing compares two guerrilla conflicts in their final eighteen months. In the first, recorded clashes fell from 60 a month to 4 while ceasefire talks ran for eleven months; in the second, clashes fell from 45 to 6 and talks ran for two. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: Fighting fell first in both cases, which suggests the talks followed rather than caused the decline.
options.misconception: reads the decline in fighting as proof talks had no effect

options.text: Fewer clashes and a longer process together suggest sustained pressure that made agreement possible.
The two conflicts show the same pattern, since a shorter process produced a faster reduction in clashes.
options.misconception: claims a shorter negotiation always worked better

options.text: Clash counts tell nothing about negotiations, since fighting levels were never recorded reliably.
options.misconception: dismisses the counts as unreliable

questions.explanation: Both conflicts show fighting falling while talks continued, and the longer process was followed by the lower final rate, which is what sustained pressure produces. The order of events and the reliability of the counts do not settle the case.
questions.hint: Read the two rows together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The end of a settler state
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the timing of majority rule varied between settler colonies.
questions.stem: A seminar compares two settler colonies where elections were introduced at different moments. Which explanation for the difference is soundest?

options.text: The later introduction reflected a settlement negotiated with settlers that kept their local authority.
options.misconception: attributes the difference to a negotiated settlement

options.text: Both introductions followed the same metropolitan timetable, so the difference was administrative.
options.misconception: claims a single timetable governed both colonies

options.text: The earlier introduction was simply a mistake by officials who acted without instruction.
options.misconception: explains the difference as official error

options.text: The strength of organised settler opposition determined how long the delay lasted in each case.

questions.explanation: Where settler interests were strongly organised, the metropole found it politically costly to press the claim, so the vote was postponed; where they were weaker it came earlier. A shared timetable and official error do not explain it.
questions.hint: Ask what made pressing the claim politically costly.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why similar colonies produced different metropolitan decisions.
questions.stem: Your archive's study room asks you to explain why a metropolitan government could accept negotiated independence in one colony while refusing it in another with similar settler numbers.

answer.exemplar: The arithmetic of empire was not the only variable that mattered. In one colony the metropolitan government could see an orderly transfer of assets, a manageable defence bill afterwards and a political settlement that let it present the change as a success, while in the other the war of independence had become a public grievance about a particular ministry's failures. Where a settled succession was available the centre chose it; where the issue had become a matter of blame at home, a settlement looked like an admission of defeat and was refused.

questions.explanation: Metropolitan decisions turned on whether an orderly succession looked like a success or an admission of failure, not on the colonial arithmetic alone. Similar settler numbers did not produce similar outcomes.
questions.hint: Ask how the outcome would be presented at home.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a settlement clause as protected title applied unevenly.

stimulus.body: The clause provides that the Commission shall certify the ownership of all lands held under valid title at the date of the transfer, and that any land not so held shall revert to the Commission for distribution. A schedule lists the districts in which certification has been completed, together with a note that the procedure has been suspended in three districts pending a further report.

questions.stem: An exhibition uses this settlement clause. What does it reveal about the balance of interests in the agreement?

options.text: The agreement redistributed all land without exception, so nothing was protected.
options.misconception: claims the clause protected nothing at all

options.text: Existing title was protected by the agreement, and its application was uneven in practice.
The clause was drafted to delay the handover by keeping ownership permanently undecided.
options.misconception: reads the certification schedule as deliberate indefinite delay

options.text: The clause removed all discretion from the commission, leaving decisions to the courts.
options.misconception: claims the clause left all discretion to the courts

questions.explanation: The clause certifies existing title and returns uncertified land to the commission, so established property was protected, and the suspended districts show protection applied unevenly. Wholesale redistribution and judicial substitution do not fit.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause protects and what the schedule reveals.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh realism against weakness in pre-handover terms.
questions.stem: A panel asks whether the terms agreed before handover were a sign of weakness or of realism in the incoming government's position.

options.text: They were realism, because a state built on paper could not be run without inherited machinery.
They were weakness, because every clause conceded by the incoming side was avoidable.
options.misconception: claims every concession was avoidable

options.text: They were weakness, since the drafts were produced by the outgoing side alone.
options.misconception: treats drafting alone as proof of weakness

options.text: They were realism, because the incoming government drafted every provision itself.
options.misconception: contradicts the drafting arrangement described

questions.explanation: Inherited machinery was what allowed a state to function at all, so settling its terms beforehand was realism about capacity rather than surrender of principle. Drafting power alone does not explain it.
questions.hint: Ask what a state could run without inherited machinery.
